name: Rational corset

lead: Rational or reform corsets emerged in the 19th century as alternatives to rigid, tightly laced stays. Designers and physicians wanted garments that supported the torso and gave a smooth line while reducing pressure on the abdomen and ribs. Worn, they change the silhouette and posture-like carriage while on.

Examples include the straight-front corset by Inès Gaches-Sarraute around 1892, which sought to reduce abdominal pressure and produced an S-curve shape, and the corsets of Roxey Ann Caplin, made with her physician husband.

paras: The wearer is fitted with a corset whose cut distributes pressure differently, often with a straight busk, and wears it under clothing. Reformers also promoted alternatives such as the liberty bodice, which hung skirts from the shoulders.

Reformers argued that tight corsets displaced organs and harmed health, and that was the motivation for the designs. Fit matters; ill-fitting corsets were the concern that led some doctors to become corset fitters.

chain: Pressure spread more evenly than tight stays
angle.text: While worn, a reform corset shapes the torso into a defined line and supports the trunk. It was designed to do so with less compression than tightlacing.

lead: The rational corset belongs to the dress reform movement of the 19th century, whose participants opposed the rigid, heavily laced Victorian corset and offered alternatives ranging from redesigned corsets to replacing the corset altogether.[1] The aim was a garment that kept a refined silhouette without the compression attributed to tight lacing.

Notable designers included Roxey Ann Caplin, a corset maker who worked with her physician husband on corsets she described as more respectful of human anatomy, and Inès Gaches-Sarraute, who around 1892 designed a straight-front corset in response to gynecological problems patients attributed to corsets.[1] Her design aimed to reduce abdominal pressure and produced the S-curve silhouette that became fashionable in the early 20th century.[1]

paras: Reformers said conventional corsets damaged and displaced internal organs, compromised fertility and weakened health overall, and Catharine Beecher discussed uterine prolapse linked to lifelong corset use.[1] Reform corsets were typically built to reduce compression, in contrast to tight-lacing, which laced to extremely small waists.[1] The physician Alice Bunker Stockham opposed corsets, especially in pregnancy.[1]

The emancipation waist or liberty bodice was a sleeveless button-front vest from which petticoats hung so the torso, not the waist, bore the weight.[1] The Rational Dress Society was founded in London in 1881 to promote practical clothing such as divided skirts.[1] Gustav Jaeger argued in 1878 for animal-hair clothing for health.[1]

Corsets were nearly universal until the 1920s, and the movement's main result was the evolution of the corset into hygienic forms rather than its disappearance.[1] Doctors became corsetieres to fit garments properly.[1]

timeline.event: Gustav Jaeger promotes animal-hair clothing for health.[1]
Rational Dress Society founded in London.[1]
